title: Lecture #27: Java Generics Deep Dive
topics: Limitations of Object as a universal type

questions.question: What is the main problem that generics solve, according to the lecture?
options: They make programs run faster by avoiding objects on the heap
They move type errors from runtime (for example a `ClassCastException`) to compile time, and remove the need for casts when reading values
They let one variable hold values of any type without any checks
They allow primitive types like `int` to be stored directly in collections
questions.explanation: With an `Object`-based `Box`, the type information is lost: anything can be inserted, reading requires a cast, and mistakes only show up at runtime. A generic `Box<Integer>` lets the compiler check every use, so wrong types are rejected before the program runs and no cast is needed. Generics still work only with reference types such as `Integer`.
questions.source: notes p3 (limitations of Object as universal type, compile time vs runtime)

questions.question: What does `Demo3.java` print?
options: `105`, `Hello`, `false`
It does not compile: `getValue()` returns `Object` and needs a cast before `+ 5`
`15`, `Hello`, `false`
`15`, `Hello`, `true`
questions.explanation: Because `b1` is a `Box<Integer>`, `getValue()` returns an `Integer`, so `b1.getValue() + 5` is numeric addition (after unboxing): 15. No cast is needed since the type parameter `T` is replaced by `Integer` for this box. The other two boxes simply return "Hello" and `false`.

questions.topic: Limitations of Object as a universal type
questions.question: Your codebase has a non-generic `Box` that stores an `Object`. Someone writes `String s = (String) b1.getValue();` where `b1` holds `10`. The code compiles, but the app crashes in production. What happened, and what prevents this?
options: The cast fails at runtime with `ClassCastException` because the value is an `Integer`; a generic `Box<Integer>` would make the wrong cast a compile-time error
The JVM converted `10` to `"10"` but ran out of memory; increasing the heap fixes it
`getValue()` returned `null` because `Object` fields cannot hold numbers; initialise the field first
Casting is not allowed on method results; store the value in a variable before casting
questions.explanation: With `Object`, the compiler cannot know what is inside the box, so it accepts the cast and the error appears only when the line runs (`Integer cannot be cast to String`). That is the "errors shift to runtime" limitation in the notes. With `Box<Integer>`, the compiler knows `getValue()` returns `Integer` and rejects the cast to `String` outright.

questions.question: What happens when `Demo.java` runs?
options: It prints `Aditya` then `10`
It does not compile, because an `Object` can never be cast to `String`
It does not compile, because `Object obj3 = 10;` mixes a primitive with an object
It prints `Aditya`, then throws `ClassCastException` at `(String) obj3`
questions.explanation: `obj2` really refers to a `String`, so downcasting it to `String` succeeds and `Aditya` is printed. `obj3` holds an autoboxed `Integer`; the compiler allows the cast from `Object` to `String` because it might be valid, but at runtime the object is not a `String`, so a `ClassCastException` is thrown. `Object obj3 = 10;` itself is fine thanks to autoboxing.

questions.question: Given `String s = "Hello";` and `Object obj = "Hello";`, which assignment requires an explicit cast to compile?
options: `Object o = s;`
`String t = obj;`
`Object o2 = new String("Hi");`
`CharSequence c = s;`
questions.explanation: Going from a specific type to a more general one (upcasting, e.g. `String` to `Object` or to the `CharSequence` interface it implements) is always safe, so it happens implicitly. Going from general to specific (downcasting) might fail, so the compiler demands an explicit `(String) obj`, and the check is repeated at runtime. The notes mark `String s = obj;` as a compiler error for this reason.
questions.source: notes p2 (upcasting: specific -> general, no casting; downcasting: compiler error without cast)

questions.question: You need a generic `Box<T>` whose `printDouble()` method calls `value.doubleValue()`. It should accept `Integer`, `Double` and `Float`, but `Box<String>` must not compile. How do you declare it?
options: `class Box<T> { ... }` and cast `value` to `Number` inside `printDouble()`
`class Box<Number> { ... }`
`class Box<T extends Number> { ... }`
`class Box<T super Number> { ... }`
questions.explanation: An upper bound `T extends Number` limits the type argument to `Number` or its subclasses (`Integer`, `Double`, `Float`, ...), and because every `T` is a `Number`, the compiler lets you call `doubleValue()` on `value` without a cast. `Box<Number>` would just declare a type parameter named `Number`, and an unbounded `T` with a cast would still accept `String` and fail at runtime. `super` cannot be used in a type parameter declaration.
questions.source: code: Demo6.java; notes p3 (Number: Integer, Double, Float allowed; String, Boolean, Student not)

questions.question: In `public static <T, U> void printPair(T first, U second)`, what is the role of `<T, U>` placed before the return type?
options: It declares two type parameters for this method only, so the compiler can infer `T` and `U` from each call's arguments
It says the method returns a `Pair<T, U>`
It refers to the type parameters of the enclosing class, which must also be named `T` and `U`
It restricts `first` and `second` to be the same type
questions.explanation: A generic method declares its own type parameters in angle brackets just before the return type. On a call like `printPair(11, 23)`, the compiler infers `T` and `U` (here both `Integer`) from the arguments, which the lecture calls type inference. The class `Demo5` itself is not generic, and `T` and `U` may be different types.

questions.question: With the bound `T extends Animal & Swimmable`, which marked line fails to compile?
options: Line A
Line B
Line C
Line D
questions.explanation: A type argument must satisfy every bound: it must be an `Animal` and also implement `Swimmable`. `Fish` satisfies both (Line A is fine), but `Dog` is an `Animal` that is not `Swimmable`, so Line B is a compile error. Inside `Box`, `T` is known to be both, so `value.display()` and `value.swim()` (Lines C and D) compile without casts.

questions.question: Which type parameter declaration is valid Java, given `class Animal`, `class Dog extends Animal` and `interface Swimmable`?
options: `class Box<T extends Swimmable & Animal>`
`class Box<T implements Swimmable extends Animal>`
`class Box<T extends Animal & Dog>`
`class Box<T extends Animal & Swimmable>`
questions.explanation: Multiple bounds are written with `extends` and `&`, and if one bound is a class it must come first, followed by interfaces. Putting the interface first is a compile error, `implements` is never used in a type parameter, and at most one bound can be a class (Java has single class inheritance), so `Animal & Dog` is invalid.

questions.question: A teammate uses the lecture's `public static <T> T getResult(T x) { return x; }` and writes `Integer y = getResult("23");`, expecting the string to be converted to a number. What actually happens?
options: It compiles and `y` becomes `23`, because `T` is inferred as `Integer` from the target type
It compiles but throws `ClassCastException` at runtime when the result is assigned
It does not compile: `T` is inferred from the argument as `String`, and a `String` result cannot be assigned to `Integer`
It compiles and `y` is `null`, because the conversion fails silently
questions.explanation: Generic methods do not convert values; they only carry the type through. The argument forces `T` to be (a supertype of) `String`, while the target `Integer` requires `T` to be an `Integer`, and no type satisfies both, so the compiler reports incompatible types. This is the compile-time safety generics provide; real conversion needs `Integer.parseInt("23")`.
